title: The Chromium glossary
description: Chromium is easier to read once you know where work lives. These 50 concepts connect processes, navigation, rendering, JavaScript, and security to the source tree.

stages.title: Meet the browser
stages.description: Start with the layers, objects, and UI frameworks that make Chromium a browser.

lede.text: On Linux, Chromium is the open-source browser project, while Google Chrome is Google's branded browser built from it.

explanation.text: Both products use the same core browser engine and process architecture.
Chrome adds Google branding, distribution, licensed media codecs, and service integrations that are not all part of Chromium.

diagram.title: Where Chromium ends and Google Chrome begins
diagram.summary: The shared engine sits in both products; Chrome adds a separate product layer.

caption.text: Both products share the Chromium engine. Google Chrome adds its own product layer around it.

locator.value: The Difference between Google Chrome and Chromium on Linux

lede.text: The content layer is Chromium's platform-neutral browser engine API for embedders such as Chrome.

explanation.text: Public interfaces in content/public expose browser concepts without importing Chrome product UI.
Browser-side implementations in content/browser coordinate frames, navigation, processes, and storage before renderers hand web content to Blink.

diagram.title: How Chrome reaches Blink through the content layer
diagram.summary: Chrome enters through the public content API, which leads to browser implementation and Blink.

caption.text: Chrome enters through content/public. Browser-side implementations then coordinate the work that reaches Blink.

lede.text: Views is Chromium's cross-platform toolkit for desktop browser controls such as tabs, toolbars, menus, and dialogs.

explanation.text: A Widget owns the native window and hosts a tree of View objects.
BrowserView composes major Chrome controls, while platform code supplies native integration and styling.

diagram.title: How BrowserView contains the browser UI
diagram.summary: BrowserView branches into the toolbar and tab strip inside one native Widget.

caption.text: A native Widget hosts BrowserView. BrowserView contains controls such as the toolbar and tab strip.

lede.text: WebContents is the browser-side container for the web content shown in a tab, window, or embedded surface.

explanation.text: It owns a NavigationController and coordinates the FrameTree that represents the page.
Attached WebContentsObserver instances receive lifecycle and navigation notifications; WebContents does not necessarily own those observers.

diagram.title: What one WebContents coordinates
diagram.summary: One WebContents coordinates navigation and frames, then notifies attached observers.

caption.text: One WebContents coordinates navigation and the frame tree. Attached observers receive its notifications.

lede.text: WebUI connects a privileged C++ controller to an internal HTML, CSS, and TypeScript page such as chrome://settings.

explanation.text: A narrow JavaScript binding sends named messages from the page to its controller.
The controller calls browser services and returns explicit callbacks without exposing those capabilities to ordinary sites.

diagram.title: How a WebUI message reaches browser code
diagram.summary: Messages cross the WebUI binding before a controller reaches browser services.

caption.text: The WebUI binding carries page messages to a C++ controller. The controller calls browser services and returns callbacks.

stages.title: Cross process boundaries
stages.description: See which process owns each job, how processes communicate, and where failures stop.

lede.text: Chromium divides browser work among operating-system processes so one compromised page does not inherit every privilege.

explanation.text: The browser process coordinates sandboxed renderers and brokers restricted resources.
GPU and Network Service processes isolate specialized code and communicate with clients through explicit IPC interfaces.

diagram.title: How Chromium divides work across processes
diagram.summary: Four peer process regions exchange only the messages needed for their jobs.

caption.text: Browser, renderer, GPU, and network processes keep separate jobs. Explicit messages connect the work that crosses their boundaries.

lede.text: The browser process is Chromium's trusted coordinator for product UI, profiles, renderer placement, and restricted resources.

explanation.text: It creates and manages child processes instead of running untrusted page code itself.
Browser-side checks validate requests before a renderer can reach files, devices, or other protected operating-system capabilities.

diagram.title: What the browser process coordinates
diagram.summary: The trusted browser process fans out to product state, renderer control, and resource brokering.

caption.text: The trusted browser process coordinates product state and renderer control. It also brokers restricted resources.

lede.text: A renderer process runs web content with Blink and V8 inside a sandboxed operating-system process.

explanation.text: It can host related frames and workers whose placement satisfies SiteInstance rules.
Browser-side Site Isolation policy decides when a cross-site document requires a different renderer.

diagram.title: What runs inside a renderer process
diagram.summary: Blink, V8, and related web contexts share a sandboxed renderer boundary.

caption.text: Blink, V8, and related web contexts run together inside one sandboxed renderer boundary.

lede.text: A page has one logical FrameTree whose root is the main frame and whose descendants represent every iframe.

explanation.text: FrameTreeNode objects keep stable positions even when their documents or renderer hosts change.
Site Isolation can place a child frame in another process without removing it from the same logical tree.

diagram.title: How logical frames span renderer processes
diagram.summary: The logical frame tree can branch across renderer process boundaries.

caption.text: The logical frame tree keeps one hierarchy even when a child frame runs in another renderer process.

lede.text: RenderFrameHost is the browser-side endpoint for a frame's current document and its renderer connection.

explanation.text: A navigation can prepare a replacement host, including one in another renderer process.
The FrameTreeNode remains stable while commit changes which RenderFrameHost is current.

diagram.title: How a frame keeps its place through a host swap
diagram.summary: Commit swaps the current host without replacing the stable frame-tree position.

caption.text: Navigation commit replaces the current RenderFrameHost. The stable FrameTreeNode keeps its position.

lede.text: A SiteInstance groups documents and workers that must be able to use synchronous web-platform access with one another.

explanation.text: Members of one SiteInstance are assigned together under Chromium's process model.
Browser policy uses the group when choosing, reusing, or isolating a renderer process.

diagram.title: How documents share a SiteInstance
diagram.summary: Related documents share a SiteInstance, which participates in renderer selection.

caption.text: Documents that need synchronous access share a SiteInstance. Chromium uses that group when selecting a renderer.

lede.text: Site Isolation uses renderer processes as security boundaries between sites, including sites embedded as iframes.

explanation.text: The browser can represent a cross-site child through a remote frame while its document runs elsewhere.
Browser-side policy restricts which site data each locked renderer may receive.

diagram.title: How the browser separates sites across processes
diagram.summary: Browser enforcement mediates communication between renderer regions locked to different sites.

caption.text: Different sites can run in separate renderer regions. Browser enforcement mediates the communication between them.

lede.text: A ProcessLock records the site or origin that a renderer process is permitted to host.

explanation.text: Browser-side security policy compares renderer requests with that lock.
Only an allowed request can reach protected data for the locked principal.

diagram.title: How a process lock guards protected data
diagram.summary: A browser-side lock check stands between a renderer claim and protected data.

caption.text: Browser-side policy compares a renderer claim with its ProcessLock before protected data can be returned.

lede.text: Mojo is Chromium's typed message system for communication across component and process boundaries.

explanation.text: A .mojom declaration generates strongly typed Remote and Receiver bindings.
Those endpoints exchange serialized messages through a pipe whose boundary remains visible in code.

diagram.title: How Mojo carries a typed cross-process message
diagram.summary: Generated endpoints exchange typed messages through an explicit Mojo transport boundary.

caption.text: A .mojom contract generates typed endpoints. Those endpoints exchange serialized messages across the Mojo transport boundary.

lede.text: Chromium can expose a capability as a Mojo service hosted in a dedicated or shared utility process.

explanation.text: The browser binds a service interface instead of linking every implementation into its own process.
The utility host applies a sandbox profile matched to the capability's resource needs.

diagram.title: How a service reaches a sandboxed utility process
diagram.summary: A service binding leads from the browser to a utility host with a selected sandbox.

caption.text: The browser binds a service interface to a utility host. That host runs under a sandbox selected for the capability.

stages.title: Follow a navigation
stages.description: Track one page load through browser policy, the network stack, storage, and service workers.

lede.text: A navigation is the browser-controlled transition from a requested URL to a committed document.

explanation.text: NavigationRequest carries redirect, response, policy, and renderer-selection state through the browser process.
Commit happens only after the response and browser checks choose a destination RenderFrameHost.

diagram.title: How a URL becomes a committed document
diagram.summary: NavigationRequest carries a URL through fetch and browser checks to document commit.

caption.text: NavigationRequest carries the URL, response, and policy state. Commit follows only after browser checks select a destination.

lede.text: NavigationThrottle lets a browser feature inspect a navigation at defined milestones before it proceeds.

explanation.text: A throttle may continue, defer, cancel, or simulate a redirect without owning the full navigation.
Deferred work resumes the same request, while cancellation prevents response processing or commit.

diagram.title: Where a navigation throttle can change progress
diagram.summary: Throttle decisions can pause, stop, redirect, or advance one navigation.

caption.text: A throttle can defer, cancel, redirect, or advance the same navigation at defined milestones.

lede.text: URLLoader is the Mojo-facing request object that streams URL response metadata and body data to a client.

explanation.text: URLLoaderFactory carries request context and decides which clients may create loaders.
The loader drives the Network Service stack, then returns the streamed response through its client endpoint.

diagram.title: How a URLLoader request returns a response
diagram.summary: The factory authorizes a loader that crosses into the network stack and streams a response back.

caption.text: URLLoaderFactory authorizes the loader. The network stack then streams the response back to its client.

lede.text: The Network Service owns most of Chromium's network stack behind Mojo interfaces and can run outside the browser process.

explanation.text: Renderer and browser clients submit requests without direct access to sockets or certificate state.
The service centralizes cookies, cache access, proxies, certificates, and transport policy on top of net.

diagram.title: How clients reach the network stack
diagram.summary: Clients reach the net stack through a separate service boundary and typed requests.

caption.text: Browser and renderer clients send typed requests across the Network Service boundary to reach the net stack.

lede.text: NetworkIsolationKey partitions Chromium's HTTP cache by the request's top-frame and frame-site context.

explanation.text: The two site values form a key used when selecting a cache partition.
Other network state and connections generally use NetworkAnonymizationKey, not NetworkIsolationKey itself.

diagram.title: How two sites form an HTTP cache key
diagram.summary: Two site inputs converge on the key that selects an HTTP cache partition.

caption.text: The top-frame site and frame site form a NetworkIsolationKey. That key selects an HTTP cache partition.

lede.text: Chromium's HTTP cache reuses stored responses only when HTTP freshness and validation rules allow it.

explanation.text: A cache lookup can return a fresh entry without a network transfer.
A stale entry or miss triggers network validation or retrieval before the cache and caller receive an updated response.

diagram.title: How the HTTP cache chooses reuse or revalidation
diagram.summary: Freshness decides whether a request reuses a response or returns through network revalidation.

caption.text: A fresh entry returns directly. A stale entry or miss goes through network validation before the response is updated.

lede.text: A cookie is sent or exposed only when it passes Chromium's inclusion rules for the current request context.

explanation.text: CookieMonster supplies stored candidates for the target URL.
Domain, path, Secure, SameSite, partitioning, and user policy determine whether each candidate is included or excluded.

diagram.title: How Chromium decides which cookies join a request
diagram.summary: Stored candidates branch at one inclusion decision before a request is assembled.

caption.text: Stored candidates pass through Chromium's inclusion rules. Only allowed cookies are attached to the request.

lede.text: An origin is a scheme, host, and port security principal; a schemeful site is a broader scheme plus registrable-domain grouping.

explanation.text: Same-origin checks protect direct web-platform access such as DOM reads.
Chromium also uses site-level grouping when making process placement and Site Isolation decisions.

diagram.title: How origins fit inside a schemeful site
diagram.summary: Multiple origins can belong to one schemeful site while retaining separate origin security checks.

caption.text: One schemeful site can contain multiple origins. Direct web-platform access still depends on the narrower origin boundary.

locator.value: Use origin (rather than URL) for security decisions.

lede.text: StoragePartition is the browser-side container for storage and network services assigned to one browsing context partition.

explanation.text: It exposes peer services such as NetworkContext, ServiceWorkerContext, and DOM storage.
Embedders and privacy features can use separate partitions so those contexts do not share the same state.

diagram.title: What a StoragePartition contains
diagram.summary: One StoragePartition contains several peer services without implying a call sequence between them.

caption.text: One StoragePartition holds network, worker, and DOM storage services as peers. Their containment does not imply a call sequence.

lede.text: A service worker is registered for an origin and scope, then runs background fetch and event code under a storage key.

explanation.text: The browser process coordinates registration, lifetime, and routing while Blink executes the worker script in a renderer.
A matching fetch event can answer from storage or request the network before returning a response to the page.

diagram.title: How a service worker answers a fetch
diagram.summary: A matching service worker can branch to storage or network before answering a page fetch.

caption.text: A matching service worker can read storage or request the network before it returns a response to the page.

stages.title: Render a frame
stages.description: Follow a document through style, layout, paint, raster, and display.

lede.text: Blink is Chromium's rendering engine and implementation of the web platform.

explanation.text: It parses HTML and CSS, exposes DOM APIs, and advances documents through style, layout, and paint.
Blink records a PaintArtifact that the compositor can turn into a displayed frame.

diagram.title: How Blink turns web input into compositor output
diagram.summary: Blink turns web input into lifecycle output that the compositor can consume.

caption.text: Blink advances HTML and CSS through the document lifecycle. The resulting paint artifact becomes compositor input.

lede.text: The DOM is Blink's live object graph for a document, including elements, text nodes, and shadow trees.

explanation.text: The HTML parser and scripts can add, remove, or mutate nodes.
A mutation marks dependent style, layout, or paint work dirty instead of drawing pixels immediately.

diagram.title: How a Document branches into DOM trees
diagram.summary: A document contains elements that can branch into light-DOM text and a shadow tree.

caption.text: A Document contains elements. An element can own light-DOM children and host a separate shadow tree.

lede.text: Style recalculation matches CSS rules and computes the resolved style for affected DOM nodes.

explanation.text: A DOM or stylesheet change produces invalidation information that narrows the work.
The style resolver combines applicable rules with inherited state and writes computed style for later layout.

diagram.title: How invalidation limits style recalculation
diagram.summary: Invalidation scopes the resolver, while CSS rules supply the inputs used to compute style.

caption.text: Invalidation narrows the nodes that need work. The style resolver combines that scope with applicable CSS rules.

lede.text: Layout converts computed style and document structure into boxes and immutable physical fragments with geometry.

explanation.text: Layout objects select algorithms for block, inline, flex, grid, and other formatting contexts.
Those algorithms produce sizes and positions that hit testing and painting can consume.

diagram.title: How styled objects become physical fragments
diagram.summary: Layout algorithms transform styled objects into positioned fragment output.

caption.text: Layout objects select the relevant algorithms. Those algorithms produce positioned physical fragments.

lede.text: Blink advances each document through ordered style, layout, pre-paint, and paint lifecycle phases.

explanation.text: Dirty flags prevent later phases from consuming stale inputs and avoid work for unchanged state.
A new mutation can mark style dirty again, closing the update cycle for a later rendering opportunity.

diagram.title: How the document lifecycle repeats
diagram.summary: Ordered lifecycle phases repeat when new document state becomes dirty.

caption.text: Style, layout, pre-paint, and paint run in order. A later mutation can mark the document dirty and start another cycle.

lede.text: Paint walks layout output and records drawing commands as display items rather than immediately filling pixels.

explanation.text: Specialized painters emit operations in paint order for relevant layout objects.
PaintController groups those items into chunks and stores them in a reusable PaintArtifact.

diagram.title: How layout output becomes a paint artifact
diagram.summary: Painting records reusable display items and groups them into one artifact.

caption.text: Painters record display items instead of pixels. PaintController groups those items into a reusable PaintArtifact.

lede.text: PaintArtifact is Blink's ordered record of display items partitioned into chunks with shared visual property state.

explanation.text: Each chunk references transform, clip, effect, and scroll information without copying the full trees.
PaintArtifactCompositor converts that record into compositor layers and property-tree state.

diagram.title: How display items become compositor input
diagram.summary: Paint chunks turn an ordered display list into input for compositor layerization.

caption.text: Paint chunks partition the ordered display list. The resulting PaintArtifact becomes input for compositor layerization.

lede.text: Paint invalidation finds recorded drawing that is no longer reusable after content or geometry changes.

explanation.text: PaintController compares new work with the previous artifact and retains matching display items or subsequences.
Changed regions are invalidated and repainted while unaffected recording remains cached.

diagram.title: How Chromium separates reusable and invalid paint
diagram.summary: A comparison splits prior paint output into reusable and invalidated work.

caption.text: PaintController compares new work with the prior artifact. Matching items stay reusable while changed regions are repainted.

lede.text: Property trees store transforms, clips, effects, and scrolling separately from the DOM and layout trees.

explanation.text: A paint chunk references one node from each relevant property tree.
Shared nodes let compositor-only changes update many chunks without rebuilding all document or paint state.

diagram.title: How a paint chunk references four property trees
diagram.summary: One paint chunk fans out to the independent property state that affects it.

caption.text: A paint chunk references independent transform, clip, effect, and scroll state without copying the full trees.

lede.text: Compositing maps painted content into layers and combines those layers into a frame.

explanation.text: Layerization uses paint chunks and property state to decide which content can move or animate independently.
Compositor-thread updates can then change scrolling or transforms without rerunning the full Blink lifecycle.

diagram.title: How paint chunks become a compositor frame
diagram.summary: Layerization converts painted chunks into independently composited frame content.

caption.text: Layerization turns paint chunks into compositor layers. Those layers combine into a compositor frame.

lede.text: Rasterization executes recorded paint operations to fill the pixel resources used by compositor tiles.

explanation.text: Chromium schedules tile tasks and prioritizes work needed for the visible viewport.
A software or GPU-backed raster path produces resources that can be assembled into a compositor frame.

diagram.title: How tile work becomes pixel resources
diagram.summary: Scheduled tile work turns recorded drawing into pixel resources for composition.

caption.text: Scheduled tile tasks send recorded drawing through a raster backend. The result is pixel resources for composition.

lede.text: Viz is Chromium's display compositor service for combining renderer and browser UI submissions.

explanation.text: Producers submit CompositorFrames into retained surfaces owned by Viz.
Viz aggregates the reachable surface graph, draws the result, and presents it through the platform display pipeline.

diagram.title: How renderer and browser frames converge in Viz
diagram.summary: Renderer and browser UI frames converge in Viz before final display.

caption.text: Renderer and browser UI frames enter Viz surfaces. Viz aggregates them before final display.

lede.text: A CompositorFrame is a submitted bundle of render passes and resources, while a Surface retains that submission for Viz aggregation.

explanation.text: A SurfaceId identifies the evolving retained slot rather than one immutable bitmap.
Viz follows references through the surface graph and combines the current frames into one aggregate.

diagram.title: How a CompositorFrame enters the surface graph
diagram.summary: A submitted frame enters an identified Surface, then participates in graph aggregation.

caption.text: A SurfaceId identifies where a submitted CompositorFrame is retained. Viz follows the surface graph to aggregate the current frames.

lede.text: BeginFrame signals tell visual producers when to update content for an upcoming display frame.

explanation.text: A BeginFrameSource derives a cadence from display timing and issues BeginFrameArgs.
The compositor performs animation and rendering work, submits a frame, and waits for the next timing pulse.

diagram.title: How display timing drives each frame
diagram.summary: Display timing drives a repeating update, submission, and presentation cadence.

caption.text: Display timing produces BeginFrameArgs. Compositors update and submit work before the next timing pulse.

lede.text: The GPU process keeps graphics-driver interaction and validated graphics command execution outside renderer processes.

explanation.text: Renderer clients write command-buffer operations that GPU service code validates before execution.
The process also supports raster, compositing, graphics APIs, and video paths that need controlled driver access.

diagram.title: How graphics commands cross the GPU boundary
diagram.summary: Command validation stands between an untrusted graphics client and the platform driver.

caption.text: Renderer commands enter the GPU process for validation. Only controlled calls reach the platform driver.

lede.text: Ozone is Chromium's interface between higher-level UI and graphics code and a platform window system.

explanation.text: Ozone backends provide windows, surfaces, input, cursor, display, and GPU integration behind common interfaces.
Chromium can target Wayland, X11, DRM, or another platform without spreading native dependencies through UI and Viz.

diagram.title: How Ozone connects Chromium to a window system
diagram.summary: Ozone keeps Chromium UI code independent from a selected native window backend.

caption.text: Chromium UI and Viz call common Ozone interfaces. A selected backend handles the native window system.

stages.title: Run and schedule JavaScript
stages.description: See where V8 runs, how Blink exposes web APIs, and how Chromium schedules work.

lede.text: V8 is the JavaScript and WebAssembly engine embedded by Chromium.

explanation.text: It parses, compiles, and executes code inside an isolate and one of its contexts.
V8 manages JavaScript memory while generated Blink bindings connect script objects to web-platform implementations.

diagram.title: How V8 turns source into execution
diagram.summary: V8 turns script source into execution within an isolate and context.

caption.text: V8 parses and compiles source. The resulting code runs inside an isolate and one of its contexts.

lede.text: A V8 isolate owns an independent runtime and heap, while each context supplies a global execution environment inside it.

explanation.text: A renderer main thread or worker thread generally runs one isolate.
That isolate can hold multiple contexts, including main-world and isolated-world globals, with Blink enforcing the relevant security boundaries.

diagram.title: How one isolate contains multiple contexts
diagram.summary: One renderer thread runs an isolate that can contain several distinct execution contexts.

caption.text: A renderer or worker thread generally runs one isolate. That isolate can contain several distinct execution contexts.

lede.text: Blink and V8 bindings expose Web IDL interfaces as JavaScript objects backed by Blink C++ implementations.

explanation.text: A generator produces glue that converts values, dispatches calls, and checks the active context.
Wrappers and native objects keep coordinated lifetimes across the JavaScript and Oilpan heaps.

diagram.title: How Web IDL reaches a Blink object
diagram.summary: Generated glue connects a Web IDL contract to a V8 wrapper and Blink implementation.

caption.text: Generated bindings turn a Web IDL contract into a V8 wrapper that bridges to the Blink implementation.

lede.text: Chromium posts units of work as tasks to TaskRunner interfaces instead of sharing arbitrary thread access.

explanation.text: A sequenced runner guarantees task order even when execution is not permanently tied to one physical thread.
Callbacks or reply tasks carry results back to the caller's sequence.

diagram.title: How work and replies preserve sequence order
diagram.summary: A TaskRunner preserves sequence ordering while work and replies cross thread boundaries.

caption.text: TaskRunner schedules work on a worker thread. A reply task returns the result while preserving sequence order.

lede.text: Blink's renderer event loop runs queued tasks, performs microtask checkpoints, and participates in rendering opportunities.

explanation.text: The renderer scheduler selects eligible task queues according to policy and frame state.
A long JavaScript task delays later microtasks, input handling, lifecycle updates, and presentation on the same main thread.

diagram.title: How the event loop returns to the next task
diagram.summary: Tasks, microtasks, and rendering opportunities share a repeating main-thread schedule.

caption.text: A task completes before the microtask checkpoint and rendering opportunity. The loop then selects another eligible task.

lede.text: Web workers run scripts outside a document's main thread under ownership and lifetime rules specific to each worker type.

explanation.text: A document creates a dedicated worker, multiple clients can connect to a shared worker, and origin events can wake a service worker.
Browser-side hosts and Blink worker threads still follow Chromium's site and process security constraints.

diagram.title: How the three worker models differ
diagram.summary: The three worker models branch by ownership, clients, and lifetime trigger.

caption.text: Dedicated, shared, and service workers differ in who creates them, who connects to them, and what keeps them alive.

lede.text: V8 collects JavaScript objects while Blink's Oilpan collector manages many C++ web-platform objects.

explanation.text: Wrappers and native objects can reference one another across the two heaps.
Unified tracing accounts for those cross-heap references so each collector can determine reachability without claiming an exact lifetime guarantee.

diagram.title: How V8 and Oilpan trace across heaps
diagram.summary: Cross-heap tracing follows references between a V8 wrapper and its Oilpan object.

caption.text: V8 wrappers and Oilpan objects can reference one another. Unified tracing follows those cross-heap references.

stages.title: Enforce security boundaries
stages.description: Understand the sandbox and Chromium's rule for placing risky code.

entries.term: Sandbox and the Rule of Two

lede.text: Chromium sandboxes processes that parse untrustworthy content so they cannot directly use high-privilege operating-system resources.

explanation.text: The Rule of Two says a component should not combine untrustworthy input, a memory-unsafe implementation, and high privilege.
A sandbox removes privilege from risky code, while a narrow browser broker mediates the resources that code still needs.

diagram.title: How the sandbox mediates resource access
diagram.summary: The sandbox and broker break the dangerous combination described by the Rule of Two.

caption.text: The sandbox removes direct privilege from risky code. A narrow browser broker mediates the resources it still needs.

stages.title: Trace the system
stages.description: Connect work across processes and threads with tracing.

lede.text: Tracing records timestamped events, counters, and flows from Chromium's processes and threads into a shared Perfetto timeline.

explanation.text: Browser, renderer, and GPU code emit categorized trace events and can connect related work with flow identifiers.
A captured trace aligns those tracks so navigation, scheduling, rendering, and memory work can be followed across subsystem boundaries.

diagram.title: How process events become one trace
diagram.summary: Events from several process tracks converge in one time-aligned trace.

caption.text: Browser, renderer, and GPU tracks emit timestamped events. Perfetto aligns them in one trace.
